units.title: Everything is made of matter
units.key_idea: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space, and it is made of tiny particles with gaps between them.
units.body:
Look around your home: the water in the matka, the air you breathe, the iron of the bucket, the wheat in the sack. All of these are matter. Matter is anything that has mass (it has weight) and takes up space.

All matter is made of extremely small pieces called particles. They are so small that we cannot see them, even with a magnifying glass.

Here is a simple test. Put a spoon of sugar into a glass of water and stir. The sugar seems to disappear, but the water tastes sweet. The sugar particles have spread into the gaps between the water particles. This tells us three things:
1. Particles of matter have space between them.
2. Particles are always moving.
3. Particles attract each other. This pull holds them together.

When you smell your mother's cooking from the courtyard, it is because tiny particles of the food's smell travel through the air and reach your nose. This spreading is called diffusion, and it is faster when things are hot.
questions: Air has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Feelings, sound and shadows are not.
What happens to sugar particles when sugar dissolves in water?
They spread into the gaps between water particles
They sink and stay as a lump
Sugar particles move into the spaces between water particles, so the water tastes sweet.
Why can we smell food cooking from far away?
Smell particles spread through the air
Tiny particles from the food spread through the air and reach us. This is diffusion.
The spreading of particles of one substance into another is called:
Diffusion is the mixing of particles because they keep moving.
Diffusion happens faster when the temperature is:
It does not depend on temperature
Heat gives particles more energy, so they move and spread faster.
Which statement about particles of matter is TRUE?
They have no space between them
They can be seen with our eyes
Particles are always moving; this is why diffusion happens.
What holds the particles of matter together?
A force of attraction between them
Particles pull on each other. This attraction keeps them together.
Has mass and takes up space
Mass and volume (space) are what make something matter.

units.title: Solid, liquid and gas
units.key_idea: Solids keep their shape, liquids take the shape of their container, and gases fill all the space they get.
units.body:
Matter around us comes in three common states: solid, liquid and gas.

A solid, like a brick or a stone, has a fixed shape and a fixed volume. Its particles are packed very close together and hold each other tightly. That is why you cannot push your hand through a wall.

A liquid, like milk or water, has a fixed volume but no fixed shape. Pour one litre of milk from a pot into a bottle and it takes the bottle's shape, but it is still one litre. Its particles are a little further apart and can slide past each other, so liquids flow.

A gas, like air or the steam from a pressure cooker, has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume. Its particles are far apart and move very fast in all directions. A gas spreads to fill any space. This is why an LPG leak can be smelled in the whole kitchen.

Because gas particles are far apart, gases can be squeezed (compressed) a lot. That is how a lot of LPG fits inside one cylinder.
questions: Which state of matter has a fixed shape?
Solids keep their shape because their particles are held tightly in place.
Milk poured from a pot into a bottle takes the bottle's shape. This shows liquids:
Liquids take the shape of the container but keep the same volume.
Why can a lot of LPG fit in one cylinder?
Gas particles have big gaps, so gases can be pushed into a small space.
In which state are particles farthest apart?
Gas particles are far apart and move freely.
Which of these has a fixed volume but no fixed shape?
Water is a liquid: fixed volume, takes the container's shape.
Their particles can slide past each other
Liquid particles are loosely held and can slide, so liquids flow.
Why can you smell an LPG leak in the whole kitchen?
Gas spreads to fill all the space
Gases spread out in every direction to fill the space.
Which is the hardest to compress?
Solid particles are packed tightly, so solids can hardly be squeezed.

units.title: Changing states: melting and evaporation
units.key_idea: Heating or cooling changes the state of matter; evaporation happens from the surface and causes cooling.
units.body:
Matter can change from one state to another when we heat it or cool it.

When ice is heated, it becomes water. This is melting. The temperature at which a solid melts is its melting point. For ice it is 0°C. When water is heated to 100°C, it boils and becomes steam. When steam cools, it turns back into water drops. You can see this on the lid of a cooking pot.

Water does not need to boil to become vapour. Wet clothes on a rope dry even on a cool day. This slow change from liquid to gas at the surface, below the boiling point, is called evaporation.

Evaporation is faster when:
1. It is hotter.
2. There is more wind.
3. The air is dry (less humidity).
4. The surface area is bigger. That is why we spread clothes out.

Evaporation also cools things. Water in a clay matka stays cool because water seeps out through tiny holes and evaporates, taking heat away from the pot. Sweat cools our body in the same way.
questions: Ice turning into water is called:
A solid changing to a liquid on heating is melting.
At what temperature does pure water boil at normal air pressure?
Pure water boils at 100°C at normal pressure.
Why does water in a clay matka stay cool?
Water evaporates from its surface and takes away heat
The matka is kept in the dark
Evaporation from the pot's surface takes heat away and cools the water.
Wet clothes dry faster on a:
Heat and wind both speed up evaporation.
Why do we spread clothes out to dry?
A bigger surface area speeds up evaporation
More surface means more water can evaporate at once.
Water drops on the inside of a pot lid come from:
Steam touches the cooler lid and turns back into water.
Evaporation is different from boiling because it:
Happens at the surface below the boiling point
Evaporation is a slow surface change that can happen at any temperature.
Why does sweating cool our body?
Sweat evaporates and takes heat from the skin
Evaporation needs heat, which it takes from our skin.

units.title: Distance and displacement
units.key_idea: Distance is the full path travelled; displacement is the straight-line gap between start and finish, with a direction.
units.body:
An object is in motion when its position changes with time. A bullock cart moving on the road is in motion. The tree beside the road is at rest.

Imagine you walk from your house to the well, 300 metres away, and then walk back home. How far did you travel? You walked 300 m + 300 m = 600 m. This total length of the path is called distance.

But where did you end up? Back at home, where you started. The straight-line gap between your starting point and finishing point is zero. This is called displacement.

Displacement has two parts: how much (a number) and which way (a direction). For example, "200 m towards the east". Distance has only a number.

So:
1. Distance = the whole path walked. It can never be less than displacement.
2. Displacement = the shortest straight line from start to end, with direction.
3. If you return to the start, displacement is zero, even if you walked a lot.
questions: You walk 300 m to the well and 300 m back home. What is your distance?
Distance adds the whole path: 300 + 300 = 600 m.
In the same trip (home to well and back), what is your displacement?
You ended where you started, so the straight-line gap is zero.
Which of these needs a direction to be complete?
Displacement has size and direction, like 200 m east.
An object is in motion when:
Motion means change of position over time.
Can distance ever be less than displacement?
Displacement is the shortest path, so distance is always equal or greater.
A goat walks 40 m east in a straight line. Its displacement is:
In one straight line, displacement equals distance with the direction: 40 m east.
Shortest straight line from start to end
Displacement measures the straight gap between start and finish.
Which is at rest compared to the road?
The tree does not change its position on the road.

units.title: Speed and velocity
units.key_idea: Speed = distance ÷ time; velocity is speed in a particular direction.
units.body:
Two friends ride bicycles to the market 6 km away. Ravi takes 30 minutes and Sita takes 20 minutes. Who is faster? Sita, because she covers the same distance in less time.

Speed tells us how fast something moves:

Speed = Distance ÷ Time

Sita's speed = 6 km ÷ 20 minutes. To get km per hour, change 20 minutes into 1/3 hour. So her speed is 6 × 3 = 18 km/h. Ravi's speed is 6 km ÷ 0.5 hour = 12 km/h.

The common units of speed are metres per second (m/s) and kilometres per hour (km/h).

On a real road a bus speeds up, slows down and stops. So we often talk about average speed: the total distance divided by the total time.

Velocity is speed in a stated direction, for example "40 km/h towards Pune". If a bus goes around a bend at the same speed, its velocity changes, because its direction changes.
questions: What is the formula for speed?
Speed tells how much distance is covered per unit of time.
A cycle goes 12 km in 1 hour. Its speed is:
A bus travels 120 km in 3 hours. Its average speed is:
Velocity includes both speed and direction.
Two riders go 6 km. Who is faster?
The one who takes less time
The one who takes more time
Less time for the same distance means more speed.
Which is a unit of speed?
Metres per second is a unit of speed.
A bus goes around a bend at a steady 30 km/h. What changes?
Direction changes, so velocity changes even if speed stays the same.
Average speed uses the whole trip's distance and time.

units.title: Acceleration
units.key_idea: Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes: (final velocity − initial velocity) ÷ time.
units.body:
When a tractor starts from rest and moves faster and faster, its velocity is changing. The rate at which velocity changes is called acceleration.

Acceleration = (Final velocity − Initial velocity) ÷ Time taken

Example: a motorbike starts from rest (0 m/s) and reaches 10 m/s in 5 seconds.
Acceleration = (10 − 0) ÷ 5 = 2 m/s². This means its velocity grows by 2 m/s every second.

The unit of acceleration is metres per second squared (m/s²).

When something slows down, like a cycle when you press the brakes, the acceleration is negative. This is also called retardation or deceleration.

If a bus moves at a steady velocity on a straight road, its acceleration is zero, because its velocity is not changing.

A mango falling from a tree speeds up as it falls. This is acceleration caused by the Earth's pull (gravity). It is about 9.8 m/s².
questions: Acceleration is the rate of change of:
Acceleration tells how fast velocity changes.
A bike goes from 0 to 10 m/s in 5 s. Its acceleration is:
What is the unit of acceleration?
Velocity (m/s) changes per second, giving m/s².
A cycle slowing down when brakes are pressed has:
Slowing down means velocity decreases, so acceleration is negative.
A bus moves at a steady 40 km/h on a straight road. Its acceleration is:
Velocity is not changing, so acceleration is zero.
Why does a falling mango speed up?
Gravity gives falling objects an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s².
A car goes from 20 m/s to 10 m/s in 5 s. Its acceleration is:
Another name for negative acceleration is:
